segments.say: Lesson 9. cap, pass elk & Consistency Models. What you really give up during a network partition, and strong versus eventual consistency in practice.

The cap theorem: if the network between your database copies breaks, you must choose to stay consistent (refuse some requests) or stay available (possibly serve stale data). Here is an analogy. Two bank branches lose their phone line. Either both stop withdrawals until the line returns (consistent), or both keep serving customers and reconcile later (available).

Why does this matter? Interviewers expect you to choose consistency per feature (payments versus likes). A few key words. Consistency: Everyone reads the latest write. Availability: Every request gets a response. Partition: Network split between nodes. Eventual consistency: Copies agree after a short while.

segments.say: Partition: the link between them breaks (it will happen in distributed systems). P is not optional.

segments.say: Mumbai withdraws 30 on Node A. Node B can't learn about it. Now choose.

segments.sec: Watch: A network partition forces a choice
segments.say: C P (consistency): B refuses reads and writes until the partition heals. Correct but unavailable. Banks, inventory counts, leader election (ZooKeeper, etcd).

segments.sec: Watch: A network partition forces a choice
segments.say: A P (availability): B answers with possibly stale data and reconciles later. Always up, but eventually consistent. Social feeds, likes, carts (Dynamo, Cassandra).

segments.sec: Watch: A network partition forces a choice
segments.say: pass elk: if Partition, choose A or C; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. Even without failures, strong consistency costs latency.

cap correctly stated. In the presence of a network Partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write, or errors) and Availability (every request gets a non-error response). "C A" isn't a real option for distributed systems, since partitions happen.

Consistency models (strong leads to weak). Linearizable / strong: behaves like a single copy. Highest latency. Sequential / causal: preserves order or cause-effect (a reply never appears before the message). Read-your-writes, monotonic reads: per-user guarantees, often all the U X needs. Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop. Fast and highly available.

Pick per feature, not per system. Payment balance, seat booking, inventory decrement leads to strong (C P). Like counts, view counts, feeds, presence leads to eventual (A P). The same product can mix both.

Say it in the interview. "Partitions are a given, so the real choice is consistency versus availability during one, and latency versus consistency otherwise (pass elk). I'd choose per feature: strong consistency for payments and inventory, eventual consistency for likes and feeds, plus read-your-writes so users always see their own changes.".

Let's compare. Bank ledger / payments: C P, never show wrong balance. Ticket / seat booking: C P, no double-booking. Social likes / views: A P, approximate is fine. Shopping cart (Dynamo paper): A P, always accept add-to-cart; merge later. ZooKeeper / etcd: C P, coordination needs one truth. Cassandra (default): A P (tunable), quorum settings shift it.

A likely interview question: Explain cap with an example. A strong answer: Two replicas lose connection. A user writes to one. Either the other refuses requests until the link heals (consistent, unavailable) or it serves possibly stale data (available, eventually consistent). Choose per feature: payments C P, likes A P.
